t: Last Remaining Integer After Alternating Deletion Operations
o: List 1..n; repeatedly alternate deleting every second number starting from the left, then every second starting from the right (keeping the element at the starting end each pass), until one remains. For n = 8: [1,3,5,7] → [3,7] → [3]. For n = 5: [1,3,5] → [1,5] → [1]. With n up to 1e15 we cannot simulate; instead track only the head element, the common step between survivors, the count, and the current direction — each pass halves the count, so O(log n) passes suffice.
k: Survivors of each pass form an arithmetic progression: track (head, step, count, direction).
Left pass keeps ceil(cnt/2) items with the head unchanged; right pass keeps floor(cnt/2) items, advancing the head by step only when cnt is odd.

a.i: After any pass the remaining numbers are equally spaced. A left-to-right pass keeps indices 0, 2, 4, ..., so head stays and count becomes ceil(cnt/2). A right-to-left pass keeps indices cnt-1, cnt-3, ...; the smallest surviving index is 1 if cnt is even (head advances by step) and 0 if cnt is odd (head stays), and count becomes floor(cnt/2). Double the step each pass and flip direction until one number remains.
s: Initialize head = 1, step = 1, cnt = n, left = true.
While cnt > 1: if left, set cnt = ceil(cnt/2); else, if cnt is odd add step to head, then set cnt = floor(cnt/2).
Double step and toggle direction each pass.
a.t: O(log n) — the count halves every pass (~50 iterations for n = 1e15)

a.i: Equivalently, a closed-form recursion: f(n) for the left-start game relates to the same game on ceil(n/2) elements with reversed roles, giving f(n) = 2*(ceil(n/2) ... ) style recurrences solved bottom-up. The iterative head/step version above is simpler and less error-prone, so this serves mainly as an interview discussion point.
s: Express the state after one left pass as the mirrored subproblem on ceil(n/2) elements.
Unroll recursively or memoize; depth is O(log n).
Prefer the iterative version in practice.

w: Hand-simulate n = 5 and n = 8 to lock down the parity rule for the right pass — this is where almost all bugs live. Note this variant keeps the starting-end element each pass, unlike LeetCode 390 which deletes it; read the statement carefully. Follow-up: return the full removal order, or generalize to deleting every k-th number (Josephus-style).
